title: Build, Buy or Teach It
segs: Chapter 31. Build, Buy or Teach It.
In the third week of August, a vendor called VaultLeaf sent two people to Sahaj: a salesman and an engineer. Imran Qureshi said that sending two was a good sign. Lakshmi Iyer said it was a worse one.

VaultLeaf sold software that found and hid personal data in text, and it sold to banks. Its pitch was polished. There was a console with graphs and a certificate on a slide. It promised to be running at Sahaj in three weeks, with an accuracy of ninety-nine percent.

Anaya asked what the ninety-nine percent was measured against. The engineer seemed to have hoped for the question. It was measured, he said, against VaultLeaf’s own benchmark. So she asked whether Sahaj could run the product against its own.
The case: the same test for everyone.

This is the first thing to do when someone offers to sell you what your team could build. It is also the thing most buyers skip. The talk usually turns on price and the demonstration, and neither of those decides the matter. What decides it is measuring the vendor’s product the way you would measure your own: on your answer key, with your kinds of text.
VaultLeaf agreed to run the two hundred and four rows. It did so in a way that suggested it didn’t often do this. A week later the figures came back.

On English identity numbers it was excellent, a little better than the guard. On Hinglish names, the thing the guard had been designed for, it found sixty-two in a hundred. On Hindi in Devanagari script it did worse, and it had no way to handle a number spelled out in words. The salesman wasn’t surprised. He said the company’s customers were mostly English-first. Anaya replied that Sahaj’s were not.

The reply also contained a second answer, and Lakshmi read it three times. The standard product sent text to VaultLeaf’s cloud for processing, in a region outside India. A private deployment, running inside Sahaj’s own systems, was available at about three times the price.
What you are really buying.

Imran stayed calm. A vendor was acceptable, he said, as long as everyone understood what the money was for. You are rarely buying the model, because most vendors use the same models. You are buying the connectors, the permissions, the record of who did what, a support contract, and a person who gets out of bed when it breaks at two in the morning. That last item is usually worth more than the licence. It is also usually left out of the sum.
He wrote four questions on the board. In his experience, these decide the matter.

Table 31.1: Four questions for build or buy, with Sahaj's answers. Is this the thing the product exists to do, or is it plumbing? Sahaj's answer: Finding personal details in Hinglish is the basis of the whole case, so Sahaj should own it. How often will it need to change? Sahaj's answer: Constantly, because the answer key grows every week and the failures come from real customers. Who is awake at two in the morning? Sahaj's answer: Nobody, as yet. There was no plan, which was worth knowing. What happens if the vendor is bought or shuts down? Sahaj's answer: Nobody at VaultLeaf could say what it would take to leave.

The team then made two-year estimates on a single sheet. Buying the private deployment came to about ₹58 lakh. Building and running the guard came to about ₹71 lakh. The difference was small enough to argue either way, so the sum did not settle it. Imran’s rule did: buy the plumbing, and build the part that makes the product different.

The plan was to build the finder, the answer key and the scoreboard. They would rent only the commodity items: hosting for the models in an Indian region, and an off-the-shelf console for the logs. Before signing anything, Anaya wrote down what she had learned to write.
Worked example: A decision with a date.

I would switch to buying if VaultLeaf reaches ninety on Hinglish names on our key, or if upkeep falls on one person for more than a fifth of their time. I would switch to building more if the price rises at the next tier. Review on 1 December.
A decision with a date on it, she had found, is far easier to reverse than one without.
What sits under the product.

On the walk back, Anaya asked Imran a question she had carried since March. Were they competing with the people who make the big models? He stopped in front of the sweet shop. Then he drew the answer on the back of an invoice, with a pen borrowed from the owner.
AI products are built in layers, and each layer rests on the one below. The whole stack is called the AI value chain. Each layer gets its advantage from something different.

Table 31.2: The layers of the AI value chain. Infrastructure. What it is: Computers, chips and the cloud. Where its advantage comes from: Scale and money. Models. What it is: Some owned by companies that sell access, some released openly. Where its advantage comes from: Scale and money. Tooling. What it is: Stores for the maps of meaning, instruments for testing and tracking. Where its advantage comes from: Scale and money, and ease of use. Applications. What it is: What people actually use. Where its advantage comes from: The workflow, the data and the trust.

Most teams, Imran said, live at the top. And at the top the model is not the advantage, because competitors can call the same one through the same door. What is hard to copy is how deeply the product is built into someone’s work, and data nobody else has.

Anaya named the corrections as an example. Each time one of Farah’s agents presses “the guard hid something I needed”, the team learns something that no competitor knows. But that holds only if the data is unique, makes the product better, and is hard to get. A data advantage that fails any of those three is just a story.

Some models are open for anyone to take. An open-weight model has its weights published. You can download it and run it on your own computers, instead of calling someone else’s. These models are usually a little behind the best closed ones. In return, they give you more control over where data goes and what it costs. You pay for that in hosting and upkeep.

For a company that has promised never to let a customer’s sentence leave the building, the choice was easy. It also answered the question in the margin of Anaya’s specification. The careful judge would be an open-weight model, running on Sahaj’s own servers.

Imran then added a word that had carried a lot of weight in the vendor’s office. Lock-in is being tied to one provider because leaving would cost too much, in rewriting, remeasuring or lost features. The remedy lies in the answer key. If your test set doesn’t depend on any vendor, switching takes days.
Teach it.

On Monday the founder, Mr. Bhatia, stopped Anaya in the corridor. He had read something on a plane. Why shouldn’t the company train its own model on Hinglish? Everyone was doing it, and it would be Sahaj’s own.

Every team gets asked this, usually in a planning meeting, and usually before anyone has said what is wrong. Saying yes commits a quarter. Saying no sounds unambitious. Anaya promised an answer by Friday.
The idea is called fine-tuning. You take a model that already exists and train it further on examples of your own. It sounds like the obvious route to a model that knows the company’s world.

Anaya had the one thing that makes the question answerable: the list of thirty-one failures from June, with their counts. She sorted each one into one of four kinds. There are four because each kind points to a different cure.

Table 31.3: Four kinds of failure and their cures. The machine does not know. What it means: The answer is missing, out of date or invented. Sahaj's count and cure: None of the thirty-one. The order numbers were an evidence problem, solved by the lookup. It knows but behaves wrongly. What it means: The content is right but the format or rule is off. Sahaj's count and cure: The eight names with "ji" after them: the machine had not been shown the convention, and a worked example fixed most of them in an afternoon. The half-hidden addresses were also format. It cannot work it out. What it means: Several steps, or real ambiguity. Sahaj's count and cure: The numbers broken across lines, which belonged to the cutting rule and not to the machine. It is right but too costly. What it means: The answer is correct and the price is wrong. Sahaj's count and cure: Not yet a problem.

Her answer to Mr. Bhatia on Friday was that fine-tuning teaches behaviour, not facts. If the complaint were that the model didn’t know Sahaj’s policy, fine-tuning would be the wrong tool. But Sahaj’s complaints were behaviours. And the team hadn’t yet tried the cheap cures. The first two could be undone in hours.

She also listed the costs that proposals leave out. Someone must create the examples and keep them current. A test set is needed first, or no one can tell whether the tuning helped, and it must never be the same as the examples the model learned from. The tuning must be redone each time the base model is retired. And the improvement lives inside one provider’s system, instead of in the instructions and the index. That is a form of lock-in.

Mr. Bhatia asked whether the answer was no. It was “not yet”, she said, and she gave the order: the instructions, then the evidence, then a smaller model, then fine-tuning. If the names with “ji” still failed after the first three, the team would teach the model. And it would know, because it had a key.

The smaller model was the option she had barely considered. Imran thought it the most likely to matter. A cheaper, faster, narrower model running in-house often decides the economics of a feature with high volume and a narrow job. Finding names in short messages was exactly such a job.
Chapter summary.

When someone offers to sell what your team could build, neither the price nor the demonstration decides it. Measuring the vendor’s product on your own answer key does. So do four questions: is it the core of what the product does, how often must it change, who is awake when it breaks, and what would it take to leave?

A good answer is often to buy the plumbing and build the part that makes the product different. Write down, with a date, the reasons that would reverse the decision. At the top of the AI value chain the model is rarely the advantage. Unique data, workflow and trust are. An open-weight model can be run on the company’s own machines. Lock-in is a cost to be measured. When a model falls short, there are four kinds of failure to tell apart. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and not facts. It comes after instructions, evidence and a smaller model, and it needs a separate test set.
